summary.text: Using Pell numbers $P_{m+2}=2P_{m+1}+P_m$ and their companion solutions to the Pell equation, the proof establishes the best-approximation bound $(\sqrt2-1)^k\le |p-q\sqrt2|$ for $0<q<P_{k+1}$; this prevents a Pell-sized shift from crossing an integer boundary and yields a signed self-similarity of the summand blocks. Summing those blocks gives a two-step recurrence, from which induction shows $a(P_{2t})=2t$ and $a(P_{2t+1})=1$, so the values at even Pell indices grow without bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 r=\sqrt2,\qquad \alpha=r-1.
\]
Then \(r^2=2\), and hence
\[
 1<r<2,
\]
so in particular \(0<\alpha<1\). Define
\[
 E(k)=\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor,
 \qquad
 u_k=(-1)^{E(k)}.
\]
For \(k\geq 1\), \(E(k)\geq0\), so this is the same exponent as the natural-number exponent used in the definition of the sequence. Thus
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n u_k.
\]
We will prove that, for the Pell numbers \(P_n\) defined below,
\[
 a(P_{2t})=2t\qquad(t\geq0).
\]
This immediately implies that \(a(n)\) is unbounded above. The main work is to establish a self-similarity of the signs \(u_k\).

Define two integer sequences by
\[
 P_0=0,\quad P_1=1,\quad P_{n+2}=2P_{n+1}+P_n,
\]
and
\[
 Q_0=1,\quad Q_1=1,\quad Q_{n+2}=2Q_{n+1}+Q_n.
\]
Thus \((P_n)=(0,1,2,5,12,\ldots)\), while \((Q_n)=(1,1,3,7,17,\ldots)\).

We first record the identities about these sequences that will be needed. Since both \(1+r\) and \(1-r\) satisfy
\[
 x^2=2x+1,
\]
a two-step induction gives
\[
 Q_n+P_n r=(1+r)^n                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 Q_n-P_n r=(1-r)^n.                                     \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, both statements are immediate for \(n=0,1\), and multiplying the relation \(x^2=2x+1\) by \(x^n\) gives exactly the same two-step recurrence as that defining \(P_n\) and \(Q_n\).

We will also use
\[
 Q_{n+1}=P_{n+1}+P_n.                                   \tag{3}
\]
This follows directly by a two-step induction from the defining recurrences. Moreover, \(P_n\geq1\) for \(n\geq1\), and
\[
 P_n<P_{n+1}\quad(n\geq0),                              \tag{4}
\]
again by induction from the recurrence.

A determinant identity is
\[
 Q_kP_{k+1}-P_kQ_{k+1}=(-1)^k.                          \tag{5}
\]
For \(k=0\), the left side is \(1\). Passing from \(k\) to \(k+1\), and using both recurrences, changes the sign of the determinant, proving (5) by induction.

We next prove the approximation estimate that drives the floor calculation.

**Approximation lemma.** If \(k\geq1\), \(p,q\in\mathbb Z\), and
\[
 0<q<P_{k+1},
\]
then
\[
 \alpha^k\leq |p-qr|.                                   \tag{6}
\]

To prove this, the two column vectors
\[
 (Q_k,P_k),\qquad (Q_{k+1},P_{k+1})
\]
form a unimodular basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\), because their determinant is \((-1)^k\) by (5). More explicitly, if \(D=(-1)^k\), then \(D^2=1\), and one can take
\[
 A=D(pP_{k+1}-Q_{k+1}q),
 \qquad
 B=D(Q_kq-P_kp).
\]
A direct expansion using (5) shows that
\[
 p=AQ_k+BQ_{k+1},
 \qquad
 q=AP_k+BP_{k+1}.                                       \tag{7}
\]
Using (2), we therefore obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 p-qr
 &=A(Q_k-P_kr)+B(Q_{k+1}-P_{k+1}r)\\
 &=(1-r)^k\bigl(A+B(1-r)\bigr).
\end{aligned}                                           \tag{8}
\]
We claim that
\[
 |A+B(1-r)|\geq1.                                       \tag{9}
\]
The inequalities on \(q\), together with (7), say
\[
 0<AP_k+BP_{k+1}<P_{k+1}.                               \tag{10}
\]
Because \(k\geq1\), we have \(1\leq P_k<P_{k+1}\). There are three cases.

* If \(B<0\), (10) forces \(A>0\); otherwise both terms in \(AP_k+BP_{k+1}\) would be nonpositive. Hence \(A\geq1\), while \(B\leq-1\). Since \(1-r<0\), we have \(B(1-r)>0\), so \(A+B(1-r)\geq1\).
* If \(B=0\), (10) gives \(A>0\), and again \(A+B(1-r)=A\geq1\).
* If \(B>0\), the upper inequality in (10) forces \(A<0\). Indeed, if \(A\geq0\), then \(B\geq1\) would give \(AP_k+BP_{k+1}\geq P_{k+1}\). Thus \(A\leq-1\), and because \(B(1-r)<0\), we get \(A+B(1-r)\leq-1\).

This proves (9). Taking absolute values in (8), and observing that \(|1-r|=r-1=\alpha\), now gives (6).

We next prove the crucial floor-shift identity. For all \(m\geq0\) and all integers \(j\) satisfying
\[
 1\leq j<P_{m+2},                                       \tag{11}
\]
we claim that
\[
 \left\lfloor(P_{m+1}+j)\alpha\right\rfloor
 =P_m+\lfloor j\alpha\rfloor.                          \tag{12}
\]

Set
\[
 x=j\alpha,
 \qquad
 \delta=\alpha^{m+1}.
\]
By (2) and (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_{m+1}\alpha
 &=P_{m+1}(r-1)\\
 &=P_m-\bigl(Q_{m+1}-P_{m+1}r\bigr)\\
 &=P_m-(1-r)^{m+1}.
\end{aligned}

aConsequently
\[
 (P_{m+1}+j)\alpha=P_m+x+w,                             \tag{13}
\]
where
\[
 w=-(1-r)^{m+1}.
\]
Since \(1-r=-\alpha\), this means
\[
 w=\begin{cases}
 \delta,&m\text{ even},\\
 -\delta,&m\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}                                            \tag{14}
\]
Thus it is enough to prove \(\lfloor x+w\rfloor=\lfloor x\rfloor\).

Write
\[
 f=x-\lfloor x\rfloor,

a
so \(0\leq f<1\). Apply the approximation lemma with
\[
 k=m+1,
 \qquad q=j,
 \qquad p=\lfloor x\rfloor+j.
\]
The hypotheses hold by (11), and
\[
 p-jr=\lfloor x\rfloor+j-jr=\lfloor x\rfloor-x=-f.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \delta\leq f.                                          \tag{15}
\]

If \(m\) is odd, then \(w=-\delta\). By (15),
\[
 \lfloor x\rfloor\leq x-\delta<x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1,
\]
so \(\lfloor x+w\rfloor=\lfloor x\rfloor\).

Suppose now that \(m\) is even, so \(w=\delta\). Apply the approximation lemma a second time, now with
\[
 p=\lfloor x\rfloor+j+1,
 \qquad q=j.
\]
Since
\[
 p-jr=\lfloor x\rfloor+1-x=1-f>0,
\]
we obtain
\[
 \delta\leq1-f.                                        \tag{16}
\]
In fact the inequality is strict. If equality held, then, because \(m+1\) is odd, (2) would give
\[
 \delta=\alpha^{m+1}=P_{m+1}r-Q_{m+1}.

a
Combining this with \(\delta=\lfloor x\rfloor+1-x\) and \(x=j(r-1)\) yields
\[
 (P_{m+1}+j)r=Q_{m+1}+\lfloor x\rfloor+1+j.             \tag{17}
\]
The right side is an integer, while \(P_{m+1}+j\) is a nonzero integer. This would make \(\sqrt2\) rational, a contradiction. For completeness, the irrationality of \(\sqrt2\) follows from the standard parity argument: if \(\sqrt2=a/b\) in lowest terms, then \(a^2=2b^2\), so \(a\) is even; substituting \(a=2c\) then shows that \(b\) is even as well, contradicting that \(a/b\) was in lowest terms.

Thus \(\delta<1-f\), and hence
\[
 \lfloor x\rfloor\leq x+\delta<\lfloor x\rfloor+1.
\]
So the floor is unchanged in the even case as well. Together with (13), this proves (12).

We now convert the floor identity into a self-similarity of the summands. From (12), for \(1\leq j<P_{m+2}\),
\[
 E(P_{m+1}+j)=P_m+E(j).                                 \tag{18}
\]
Both terms on the right are nonnegative. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 u_{P_{m+1}+j}
 &=(-1)^{E(P_{m+1}+j)}\\
 &=(-1)^{P_m}(-1)^{E(j)}\\
 &=(-1)^{P_m}u_j.                                       \tag{19}
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing (19) from \(j=1\) through \(j=M\), for any \(0\leq M<P_{m+2}\), gives
\[
 a(P_{m+1}+M)
 =a(P_{m+1})+(-1)^{P_m}a(M).                            \tag{20}
\]
For \(M=0\) this is immediate; for \(M>0\), it follows simply by splitting the defining sum for \(a(P_{m+1}+M)\) at \(P_{m+1}\) and using (19) term by term.

Let
\[
 b_m=a(P_m).
\]
We derive a two-step recurrence for \(b_m\). Since
\[
 P_{m+2}=P_{m+1}+(P_{m+1}+P_m),

a
and \(P_{m+1}+P_m<P_{m+2}\), formula (20), first with \(M=P_{m+1}+P_m\), gives
\[
 b_{m+2}
 =b_{m+1}+(-1)^{P_m}a(P_{m+1}+P_m).                    \tag{21}
\]
Applying (20) again, now with \(M=P_m\), gives
\[
 a(P_{m+1}+P_m)=b_{m+1}+(-1)^{P_m}b_m.                 \tag{22}
\]
Substitution into (21), together with \(((-1)^{P_m})^2=1\), yields
\[
 b_{m+2}=\bigl(1+(-1)^{P_m}\bigr)b_{m+1}+b_m.          \tag{23}
\]

The parity of \(P_m\) is the same as that of \(m\). Equivalently,
\[
 (-1)^{P_m}=(-1)^m.                                    \tag{24}
\]
This follows by a two-step induction: it is true for \(P_0=0\) and \(P_1=1\), and
\[
 P_{m+2}=2P_{m+1}+P_m\equiv P_m\pmod2.

a
Hence (23) alternates between
\[
 b_{m+2}=2b_{m+1}+b_m\quad(m\text{ even})              \tag{25}
\]
and
\[
 b_{m+2}=b_m\quad(m\text{ odd}).                       \tag{26}
\]

We now prove by induction on \(t\) that
\[
 b_{2t}=2t,
 \qquad
 b_{2t+1}=1.                                            \tag{27}
\]
For \(t=0\), \(P_0=0\), so \(b_0=a(0)=0\). Also \(P_1=1\), and
\[
 E(1)=\lfloor\sqrt2-1\rfloor=0,

a
so \(b_1=a(1)=1\).

Assume (27) at \(t\). Using (25) with \(m=2t\),
\[
 b_{2t+2}=2b_{2t+1}+b_{2t}=2+2t=2(t+1).

a
Using (26) with \(m=2t+1\),
\[
 b_{2t+3}=b_{2t+1}=1.

a
This proves (27) for every \(t\geq0\).

Finally, let \(M\) be any integer. Choose
\[
 t=\max(M,0)+1,

a
regarded as a positive integer, and set \(n=P_{2t}\). By (27),
\[
 a(n)=a(P_{2t})=2t>M.

a
Indeed, if \(M\geq0\), then \(2(M+1)>M\), while if \(M<0\), any positive value is greater than \(M\). Thus for every integer \(M\) there exists \(n\) with \(a(n)>M\), proving that the sequence is unbounded above.
